At the cyber café in Satara, with the fan clicking overhead, Ojas opened the job pages of three companies he wanted: two logistics firms in Pune and a farm-tech startup. He read each posting slowly and copied the repeating phrases into his notebook: 'cleaning messy data', 'dashboards', 'deployed to the cloud'.
'Look at this,' he said to Sangeeta, his cousin, who ran the café counter. 'Not one of them asks for a calculator app.'
'You have ten of those on your page.'
'Ten. All from tutorials.' He crossed them out one by one. 'So what would they want to see? Something with real, messy data. Something that's actually running online.'
He wrote two lines: a dashboard of mandi onion prices from public records, cleaned and charted; and a bus-pass renewal tracker for his college, deployed with a live link. Two projects instead of ten.
Sangeeta read it over his shoulder. 'Onion prices? Our uncle will use that.'

Mentoring notes – Jahnavi, alumni mentor

Hi Leela,
You asked how I finally finished my portfolio after putting it off all semester. The trick was stupidly simple: I stopped doing it in bits.
Before, I'd write half a project summary between assignments, lose the thread, and start again the next week. Screenshots were worse: I'd open one project, take one picture, then get pulled into a lab report.
So I blocked last Sunday, 9 to 5, phone in the drawer. Morning: I wrote all four summaries back to back, same format, and they came out more consistent than anything I'd done in pieces. After lunch: I ran each project once and took all the screenshots in one go, same window size, same zoom. By 4:30 everything was uploaded.
Four months of 'I'll do it later', finished in one day.
Try it before your placement season starts.
Kunal

qa.q: What else could Payal track to keep improving the site?

subtype: Approach: tracking which pieces get attention [Revision]
passage:
Week 1, Monday. Gargi sends her portfolio link to eight recruiters and turns on a simple visit counter. She is proudest of the long write-up about her sorting-algorithm study.
Week 3, Friday. She checks the counter with her friend Aadhya. Fourteen visits. Twelve went straight to the weather-alert app, the only project with a live demo. The algorithm write-up: one visit, eleven seconds.
'Ouch,' Aadhya says.
'No, it's useful,' Gargi says slowly. 'They want something they can click.'
Week 5, Sunday. The weather-alert app now sits at the top of the page. Gargi has spent two weekends putting her attendance tracker online as well, with a 'try it' button. The algorithm study is still there, lower down. That night the counter shows three new visits, all to the live projects.

qa.q: How long did the one visit to the algorithm write-up last?
qa.a: One visit, eleven seconds.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she saw the algorithm write-up got one visit?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed, since it was her proudest piece, but she turned that into curiosity and called the numbers useful.

qa.q: What would you change next if Gargi still wants the algorithm study noticed?
qa.a: Add a small live demo or an interactive chart to it, so it becomes something recruiters can click like the other two.

qa.q: How does the counter look to Aadhya on Friday?
qa.a: Aadhya first sees it as a blow, saying 'Ouch', then watches Gargi treat it as information.

grounding: Shows a student seeing that recruiters open only the live project, moving it to the top and putting a second project online.
